title: look at something bigger than you today
hookLine: look at something bigger than you today
tomorrow: every tradition says it: you can't do this alone

lines: THE OCEAN, A STORM, THE STARS.
FOR A SECOND, THE SELF GOES QUIET.
cards: The ocean, seen for the first time. A storm rolling in over a field. A night sky far from any city, so full of stars it looks fake.
A newborn's hand. Moments like these can stop a person in their tracks. For a second, the self goes quiet.
The problems don't vanish; they just get smaller, because something else got very big. And it's easy to go weeks without one, eyes down: on screens, on sidewalks, on lists.

teach.h: ONE NIGHT IN A THOUSAND YEARS.
teach.b: In 1836, the American writer Ralph Waldo Emerson asked his readers to imagine something: "If the stars should appear one night in a thousand years, how would men believe and adore".
His point is that they do appear, every clear night. The wonder is always on offer, to anyone who looks up.

A psalm looked at the same night sky, long before: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" Notice the move.
Look at the vast thing, and the question comes back to you: how small I am, and how strange that I'm here at all. Now the lab.

Researchers who study awe, including the psychologist Dacher Keltner at Berkeley, find it has a signature: people describe feeling small, and it isn't a bad feeling. The self shrinks, and the world opens.
In one study, people spent one minute looking up at a grove of very tall eucalyptus trees, while others looked up at a tall building.

teach.h: THE TREES AND THE DROPPED PENS.
teach.b: Then a researcher stumbled and dropped a handful of pens. The people who'd been looking at the trees picked up more of them. One minute of awe, and people were a little more helpful.
Some astronauts who've seen the whole earth from space describe a version of this too. An essayist, a psalmist, a lab: very different beliefs about what's behind the stars, and the same move.
Look up, and come back down a little different.

how: Some people seek awe on purpose: through walks in nature, stargazing, pilgrimages to mountains and great buildings, or by pausing, as the Psalms do, to consider the night sky.

games.q: you've just spent one minute looking up at giant eucalyptus trees. a stranger stumbles and drops a handful of pens. what does the study find?
o: you pick up more pens than people who looked at a building.
you pick up fewer, still lost in the trees.
games.why: the people who'd looked up at the trees helped more. one minute of awe, and people were a little more helpful.

practice: Here's the practice. If you can, look out a window, or step outside. Find the biggest thing you can see: the sky, a tree, a building, the clouds.
If you're stuck inside, close your eyes and remember the biggest thing you've ever stood under. For about seventy-five seconds, just look. Let it be big.
Let yourself be small next to it. You don't need to name what you feel.

wordCard.voice: Awe. The feeling of standing next to something vast, and getting a little smaller, and a little more generous. Nineteenth word.

carryVoice: Your line: look up. The sky is free, and it's there every night. Day nineteen.
